learningObjective: Analyze GEMV as memory-bound; understand coalescing in the one-warp-per-row layout.

canonicalClaims.claim: FP32 GEMV has arithmetic intensity ~0.25 FLOPs/byte (one FMA per FP32 load from A, amortized load from x); on Ampere and later, this is far below the compute:bandwidth balance, making GEMV memory-bound. In a one-warp-per-row layout, consecutive lanes read consecutive elements of the row, giving coalesced global-memory access.
conditions: FP32 without Tensor Core use; row-major A; warp iterates K in strides of 32.
nonImplications: Does not imply this is the fastest GEMV variant.
Does not imply x's redundant loads are always a bottleneck.

misconceptions.claim: GEMV is compute-bound at large K.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Arithmetic intensity is O(1) FLOPs/byte regardless of K; compute:bandwidth ratio determines the bottleneck.

misconceptions.claim: One-warp-per-row A access is stride-32 and non-coalesced.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Within one iteration of the loop, lanes 0..31 read A[row*K + 0..31] — stride 1 across the warp.

misconceptions.claim: The redundant x reads cause shared-memory bank conflicts.
misconceptions.whyWrong: No SMEM is used in this kernel; bank conflicts do not apply.

misconceptions.claim: GEMV cannot benefit from Tensor Cores.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Modern kernels use MMA/TC for tall-skinny GEMMs including GEMV variants (with careful shape handling).

implementationFacts: Alternative: block-parallel over K with cross-block reduction via atomic or two-stage kernels.
performanceScenarios: For very small K, GEMV can be launch-overhead-bound; for very large K, memory bandwidth from A dominates.
